newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica seen not needing 96/97 bread wheat imports.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica seen not needing 96/97 bread wheat imports.

text.p: For the first time in eight years South Africa may not need imported wheat for breadmaking following a bumper crop this season, industry sources said on Wednesday.

Latest official crop estimates forecast wheat production in the 1996/97 season (November-October) at 2.593 million tonnes, compared with commercial milling needs of around 2.462 million tonnes. Last season's crop totalled 1.969 million tonnes.

"The feeling at the moment is that there is enough wheat for us to mill this year," said Hilton Zunckel, the financial manager at the Chamber of Milling, a non-statutory body with wheat millers as members.

He said the final crop estimate is expected in the second week of February, but that there was little chance that the figure would be revised down much, despite concerns of late rain damage in some areas.

"There was concern initially that the Western Cape (crop) was rain damaged...but it has not been so severe that it has gone to animal feed," he said. The Western Cape province is South Africa's chief wheat-growing region.
A Wheat Board spokesman said the harvest in the Cape had been very late, finishing only in the first two weeks of January when it should have ended in the middle of November.

"In the Western Cape they were experiencing winter weather until the middle of December...(but) we do expect a good crop. There is a chance that we might not have to import at all," the spokesman said.
Winter months usually run from May to end-August.

The spokesman said the last time South Africa did not import wheat was in the 1988/89 season. Since then imports have ranged from a low of 257,852 tonnes in 1991/92 to a high of over a million tonnes in the 1992/93 season.
The Chamber of Milling's Zunckel said a small amount of breadmaking wheat had, however, already been imported this season.
"Initially it was not the board's position that there would be enough wheat, so some people did start their import programmes," he said, estimating the amount at around 50,000 tonnes.

He said around 30,000 tonnes of durum wheat, a hard grain used for making pasta, would have to be imported. It is traditionally sourced from France. Some 40,000-50,000 tonnes of soft wheat used for biscuit-making would also be imported.
Zunckel said there was a chance that South Africa would be able to export some wheat, with Botswana and Swaziland the most likely target markets.
South Africa's wheat import market was deregulated in May 1995 and millers have since been free to source their own grains overseas. The Wheat Board previously controlled all imports.
The Board still runs a single channel market domestically, one of the last in South Africa, which will fall away at the end of the current season following recent deregulation legislation.
